source.title: Understanding training and generalization in deep learning by Fourier analysis

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses memorization and generalization and cites studies of random-label fitting, but its own experiments do not test random labels or the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The discussion of random-label fitting and label-corruption convergence time attributes those findings to Zhang et al. (2016); the discussion of learning patterns before memorizing attributes findings to Arpit et al. (2017). Neither is a result of this study. Its experiments use natural-image and MNIST data, not randomized labels or unstructured inputs.
record.test_reason: The study explains previously reported random-label findings through Fourier analysis, but its own results measure frequency convergence and initialization effects on structured functions, natural images and true-label MNIST. They do not establish any claim version. Low-frequency-first learning alone does not measure learning real labels before memorizing noise.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors argue that gradient training prioritizes low-frequency components under suitable conditions and that small weight initialization favors generalization while retaining expressive capacity. Their generalization explanation depends on training data capturing the target's important frequencies. They offer a theoretical interpretation of earlier random-label results, without directly testing them.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes Fourier-frequency training dynamics and initialization effects on natural-image and MNIST tasks; it does not apply the original random-label intervention or measure its outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale changes generalization in the reported natural-image and MNIST experiments; weight initialization has a stronger effect than bias initialization in the MNIST experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: Small initialization produces similar training and test errors on natural-image interpolation; large initialization fits training pixels but yields noisy test outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale affects generalization in the tested natural-image interpolation task.

fits_no_version.finding: Both MNIST weight-initialization conditions achieve high training accuracy, while smaller weights yield higher test accuracy. Large bias initialization modestly slows training and lowers accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight initialization strongly affects generalization in the tested tanh MNIST network; bias initialization has a smaller effect.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorems and frequency-convergence experiments show preferential learning of low frequencies under stated conditions; high-frequency-dominant targets can cause oscillation and interference between frequencies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient training exhibits a conditional frequency preference that depends on initialization and the target spectrum.

record.problems: The experiments reported for generalization use natural-image and MNIST data rather than randomized labels. MNIST accuracy comparisons are shown in figures without exact values in the text. The paper itself notes limitations in analyzing different DNN structures and the behavior around local minima and saddle points.
record.rows_left_out: No results over the 60-row limit. Cited findings about random-label memorization, label-corruption convergence time, and learning simple patterns before memorizing are excluded because they are attributed to prior work.

untested.parts: Fitting completely random labels to near-zero training error with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, with chance test performance.
Relative training time for random and true labels, and convergence time across label-corruption fractions.
Zero-error fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steadily worsening test performance across increasing random-label corruption.
Whether weight decay, dropout and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Learning real-data patterns before memorizing noisy labels, and direct comparisons of real-label and random-label learning trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: Section 6 goes beyond citation by proposing a mechanism for earlier noise-versus-real-data findings, which warrants discusses rather than cites_only. The constructed high-frequency target in Appendix E is neither randomly labeled data nor an unstructured-input experiment.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label training error and test error at chance; whether the same networks generalize well on true labels after random-label training.
Training time for random versus true labels and its change with label corruption.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error as label corruption varies from none to all.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.
Whether networks learn real-data patterns before memorizing noise or random labels.

rows.subject: DNN with width 500-400-300-200-200-100-100
rows.operation_detail: Trained to fit a natural image using pixels with odd horizontal indexes as training data; small initialization, standard deviation 0.08.

conditions.value: all pixels whose horizontal indexes are odd

rows.measure: Test error relative to training error
rows.value: the test error is very close to the training error
rows.note: True image data; this does not test fitting random labels.
rows.check: The reported train–test error comparison is accurate, but it measures natural-image interpolation, not any version's effect; observed is therefore inappropriate here.

rows.subject: DNN with width 800-400-200-100
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with weight and bias initialization standard deviations (0.01, 0.01).
rows.measure: Prediction accuracy on training and test data over epochs
rows.note: The text says training accuracy is high and test accuracy is much higher than for the large-weight initialization condition; exact values are only shown in the figure.
rows.check: True-label MNIST accuracy under small initialization does not measure any version. The text establishes high training accuracy and better test accuracy than large initialization, although exact values are unavailable.

rows.subject: DNN with width 800-400-200-100
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with weight and bias initialization standard deviations (0.3, 0.01).
rows.measure: Prediction accuracy on training and test data over epochs
rows.note: The text says training accuracy is high and test accuracy is much lower than for the small-weight initialization condition; exact values are only shown in the figure.
rows.check: True-label MNIST accuracy under large initialization does not measure any version. The text establishes high training accuracy and worse test accuracy than small initialization.

rows.subject: DNN with width 800-400-200-100
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with weight and bias initialization standard deviations (0.01, 2.5).
rows.measure: Prediction accuracy on training and test data over epochs
rows.value: figure only; a bit slower training course and a bit lower prediction accuracy
rows.note: Compared with the (0.01, 0.01) initialization, the text describes a modest decrease; this is a true-label MNIST experiment.
rows.check: The modest slowdown and accuracy decrease concern bias initialization on true-label MNIST, not random-label optimization or another version; partial is inappropriate.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
